name: Belief bias
statement: Asked whether a conclusion follows from its premises, people accept believable conclusions and reject unbelievable ones, whatever the logic says.
meaning: The claim comes in two parts, and they have had very different fates. The first is a main effect: across a set of syllogisms, believable conclusions are endorsed more often than unbelievable ones, holding validity constant. The second is an interaction. Logic appears to count for more when the conclusion is unbelievable than when it is believable, which is read as belief degrading the quality of reasoning rather than merely tilting the answer. That second part is what three decades of theory was built to explain, and it is measured by a contrast of contrasts: the acceptance rate for valid arguments minus the rate for invalid ones, compared across believable and unbelievable material.

origin.who: J. St. B. T. Evans, Julie L. Barston and Paul Pollard
origin.note: Three experiments at Plymouth Polytechnic. The paper reviews about a dozen earlier claims of the effect, the oldest by Wilkins in 1928, and argues that most were open to criticism for weak effects, poor wording or uncontrolled carryover, so it set out to show the effect under controls for premise conversion and for two response biases.

evidence: Participants read a syllogism and judged whether the conclusion followed. Each experiment crossed validity with believability, giving four problem types. In Experiment 1, with 24 participants, the percentages accepting the conclusion were 92 for valid and believable, 46 for valid and unbelievable, 92 for invalid and believable, and 8 for invalid and unbelievable. Validity made no difference at all on believable material in that experiment. Participants were correct on 92% of problems where logic agreed with belief and 27% where the two conflicted. Experiment 2, with 64 participants in four groups of 16, gave 86, 62, 66 and 13, and correctness of 87% against 48%. Experiment 3, with 32 participants, gave 91, 53, 67 and 6, and correctness of 97% against 43%. Belief and validity were both significant in all three experiments. The interaction was significant in the first two and fell short in the third at p = .067. Verbal protocols were recorded throughout, and participants who mentioned the premises reasoned better than those who worked from the conclusion.

replication.headline: The endorsement pattern comes out the same way every time it is run; whether it shows belief damaging reasoning or only lowering the bar for saying "valid" is still argued.
replication.detail: Dube, Rotello and Heit put the contrast of contrasts on trial. Using it assumes a threshold model, which implies a straight receiver operating characteristic. They ran three experiments collecting confidence ratings alongside the valid or invalid judgement, and the empirical curves were bowed rather than straight in every case. Their Experiment 2, with 38 participants, produced the classic result by the classic method, an interaction of validity and believability at F(1, 37) = 6.50, p < .05, eta squared = .150. The same responses, scored as area under the curve, showed no accuracy difference at all, z = 0.62, p = .54, and the signal detection accuracy measure da stood at 0.71 for believable and 0.79 for unbelievable material. They concluded that the accuracy effect is a Type I error and that belief moves the response criterion. Klauer and Kellen replied that the curve is straight for the binary judgements most of the field collects, that their own multinomial model fits the old data better, and that belief bias is more than a response bias. Later work has gone both ways. Trippas, Verde and Handley built a forced choice task that holds response bias constant: their first two experiments found no belief bias, and when only one set of premises was visible at a time, unbelievable conclusions were judged more accurately, which is an accuracy effect. Stephens, Dunn and Hayes fitted a two-step signal detection model to two experiments and found a criterion shift and no discriminability difference, including when believability was varied between groups. The largest single test is a hierarchical Bayesian meta-analysis of 22 confidence-rating studies, 993 participants, by Trippas, Kellen, Singmann, Pennycook, Koehler, Fugelsang and Dubé. It found the curves not systematically asymmetric, with Bayes factors of 17.28 and 11.84 favouring near-equal variance for believable and unbelievable material, and no unconditional effect of believability on discriminability. It also found the effect is conditional. Reanalysing one study of 191 participants, 182 of whom had Cognitive Reflection Test scores, gave a three-way interaction of logic, belief and test score at -.07, 95% credible interval -.10 to -.03. Participants who got at least one test item right discriminated better on unbelievable syllogisms, d' = 1.38 [1.20, 1.56], than on believable ones, d' = .91 [.81, 1.02]. Those who got none right showed the reverse and smaller, .49 [.29, .69] against .55 [.44, .66].

study.cite: Trippas, D., Kellen, D., Singmann, H., Pennycook, G., Koehler, D. J., Fugelsang, J. A., & Dubé, C. (2018). Characterizing belief bias in syllogistic reasoning: A hierarchical Bayesian meta-analysis of ROC data. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 25(6), 2141-2174.

limits: No multi-laboratory replication of Evans, Barston and Pollard's own protocol was located. Searches of Crossref, PubMed and the reference lists of the signal detection papers turned up reanalyses, new experiments and one meta-analysis, and no coordinated many-labs project on belief bias. The meta-analysis pools studies that collected confidence ratings, which is not the binary task the older literature ran, and its own authors present the individual-differences result as a reanalysis of a single study rather than as a pooled finding. The materials are almost all English-language syllogisms given to undergraduates or online panels. Training the bias away is hard. Boissin, Caparos and De Neys ran three preregistered studies on Prolific, 99 participants in the first and 102 in the second, in which a single explanation of the problem structure raised accuracy on conflict problems by 7.3 points for initial answers and 11.0 points for final ones, while accuracy on the easy no-conflict control problems fell by 9.7 and 8.9 points. Some 41.7% of the training group gave mostly incorrect answers before and after. The authors report that the same intervention has raised accuracy by up to 58.3 points on numerical problems in their earlier work, a figure quoted here from their description of it.
misreadings: The dispute is not about whether the data replicate. Rotello, Heit and Dubé use deductive reasoning as one of four textbook cases in which an effect reproduces easily and consistently and is read wrongly anyway, and they make the point that collecting more data does not correct an error of this kind. Nor does "belief bias is a response bias" mean nothing happens. Believable conclusions are endorsed more often in every study on both sides of the argument, including Dube, Rotello and Heit's own. What is contested is which parameter moves. A second misreading is that people ignore logic. Evans, Barston and Pollard found large effects of validity alongside the belief effects, and in their third experiment participants were right 97% of the time when the two agreed. There is also no single set of four percentages to quote from the 1983 paper. Its Tables 2, 4 and 6 report three separate sets, one per experiment, and they differ. The invalid-believable cell alone runs 92, 66 and 67.
